title: How to Fix a Project That’s Spiraling Out of Control
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni offers a sequence for rescuing a project that has gone off the rails, framed around emotional intelligence. She begins by admitting the chaos, listening to the team, listing the issues and containing them the way firefighters contain a wildfire. She then treats the list as symptoms and digs for causes, using a story of a software project whose unexamined business processes were uncovered through empathic listening. Before acting she recommends a cooling-off period drawn from Goleman, so the response is not driven by anger or resentment. She closes by conceding that some projects cannot be saved and that knowing when to cut losses is itself an emotionally intelligent act.
points: Recognition and listening come first: a leader has to read the project's mood before any fix will land.
Contain the problems before solving them, as firefighters do, so the list of issues stops growing.
Treat the issue list as symptoms and ask whether the root is scope creep, bad planning or a bad idea.
A deliberate cooling-off period, following Goleman, keeps frustration from driving the turnaround plan.
Some projects should be stopped; accepting that honestly is presented as emotional maturity.
quotes: First, you need to recognize the chaos. If you keep humming along pretending everything is "fine," it will keep burning.
Be the empathy catalyst here. Listen, observe, and get a pulse on the project's mood from those around you.
Before it can be put out completely, though, they work to contain it. Have you ever seen news stories that say a wildfire is 10%, 50% contained, etc.? Think of your project the same way.
I sat down with them, engaged in empathic listening, shut up, took notes, and asked clarifying questions.
It turns out we were missing a lot. A whole set of processes was never even touched on or discussed at the project's inception.
Taking a moment to cool off allows creativity to pop in and moments of relaxation. Why put out the fire with fire? Cool off first.
But know when to cut your losses and back off. Being realistic, accepting a failure, and forging forward is a sign of emotional intelligence.
